text:
kevin: Heads up — noticed a weird latency drift in pool-a during the 22:10 scale-in. p95 looks normal but p99 jumped ~3x for about 90s. attaching timeline + a snippet of logs below.

autoscaler-bot: scale_in triggered group=pool-a reason=low_util target_replicas=4 -> 2 (policy=conservative)

kevin: timeline: scale_in start 22:09:57, first inflight drain 22:10:04, kernel handoff start 22:10:10, p99 spike window 22:10:12-22:11:45, new replicas ready 22:11:30.

anna: can you paste a perf profile or the qps shape? do we have microbatch distribution?

kevin: qps was steady ~450 rps. microbatch median 1, p50 seq 64, p99 seq ~180. Attached small profile (snippet):

```
# perf sample (aggregated)
kernel_select() +14.2%  runtime_main
batch_scheduler() +23.4%  runtime_main
kv_cache_lookup() +9.1%  runtime_main
kv_cache_miss_handling() +17.6%  runtime_main
context_switch_wait() +12.3%  runtime_main
```

mike: interesting — kernel_select and kv miss handling both high. sounds like inflight requests got routed to a node that had cold KV state and a different kernel path (fallback to generic GEMM).

julia: any evidence of aggressive preremptive scaling or eviction? our shrink policy does connection draining but doesn't wait for kernel-prober to finish.

kevin: exact log lines: 
`22:10:09 [pool-a/node-17] kernel_probe: chosen=opt_x8 seqlen_hint=64 fallback=false`
`22:10:11 [pool-a/node-09] kernel_probe: chosen=opt_x4 seqlen_hint=128 fallback=true`
`22:10:12 [pool-a/node-09] kv_cache: miss for prefix_id=0x7f3, fetching from remote`
`22:10:13 [pool-a/node-09] batch_enter: combined_batch_size=6 microbatch_sizes=[1,1,1,1,1,1]`

anna: so node-09 got a different kernel and had to do remote KV fetch -> batching didn't help because microbatches were tiny. that fits latency spike.

mike: question — why did kernel selection differ? should be deterministic for same model+seqlen_hint. are we seeing prober triggers because of backlog reshuffling during scale-in?

kevin: hypothesis: inflight queue drift during drain caused new routing decisions; batch_scheduler sampled seqlen from queued requests (higher variance) and prober ran on node-09 after a few larger seqs forced fallback. Also KV eviction happened earlier that minute (mem pressure).

julia: actionable: can we (1) make kernel selection sticky per model instance for X seconds, (2) delay scale-in until kernel_prober quiescent, or (3) change drain to prefer keeping nodes with warmed KV? Which has lowest risk?

anna: preference order: 3 (prefer warmed nodes) > 1 (sticky kernels) > 2 (delay scale-in) — delaying scale-in hurts cost and capacity planner. preferring warmed nodes could be a small scheduler tweak.

kevin: also a short-term mitigation: if batch sizes are mostly 1, enable "hold-and-merge" for 250ms during scale events to increase effective batch and avoid many microbatches hitting fallback kernels. cheap knob to try.

mike: logging/monitoring asks: add a per-node metric: kernel_variant_change_rate and kv_miss_rate per-second. add an alert if kernel_variant_change_rate > 0.05 over 1m during scale events.

autoscaler-bot: note: next scheduled scale_check at 22:20:00.

kevin: I'll open an RFC with perf graphs and propose scheduler preference change + hold-and-merge flag. can someone triage KV eviction root cause?

julia: I'll take KV eviction. likely related to a GC sweep in the COW buffer at 22:08. grabbing heapdump.

anna: I'll prototype the hold-and-merge patch and a sticky-kernel TTL (30s). can run A/B on pool-b.

mike: I'll add the metrics/alert. can we also capture a small end-to-end trace when the next scale-in happens? span names: scale_in, kernel_probe, kv_fetch_remote, batch_enter.

kevin: thanks. summary: cause=draining-induced routing + KV eviction -> kernel fallback + tiny microbatches -> p99 spike. actions=prefer-warmed-nodes scheduler, hold-and-merge during events, sticky-kernel TTL, metrics+trace.

anna: :thumbsup:

julia: noted. will post updates in this thread.

kevin: posting raw aggregated profile and a short flamegraph link: https://internal.redwood/perf/1798509999/graph
